zh_title: 军方缺乏改善弹药库存的“总体计划”——部分原因是这不是任何人的工作
summary: 根据政府问责办公室周四发布的一份研究报告，国防部没有确定、实现或衡量其在实现长期弹药生产目标方面取得的进展的“总体计划”，该研究称军方对全球事件过于敏感，并且没有准备好预测自己的需求。美国政府问责局指出，除其他问题外，武器库存缺乏集中权力，武器库存已因伊朗战争而耗尽，对美国与中国发生潜在冲突的计划至关重要。问题的核心在于军队可以购买的东西和实际需要的东西之间的差异。
content:
根据政府问责办公室周四发布的一份研究报告，国防部没有确定、实现或衡量其在实现长期弹药生产目标方面取得的进展的“总体计划”，该研究称军方对全球事件过于敏感，并且没有准备好预测自己的需求。美国政府问责局指出，除其他问题外，武器库存缺乏集中权力，武器库存已因伊朗战争而耗尽，对美国与中国发生潜在冲突的计划至关重要。问题的核心在于军方可以购买的东西与实际需要的东西之间存在差异，政府问责局表示，这甚至可能导致弹药投资超出五角大楼的要求。该报告的作者写道：“虽然国防部正在采取措施关注弹药短缺问题，但它无法解决这些差距。” “国防部没有总体计划，也没有指定和授权的领导层来改善弹药库存并满足其弹药需求。由于没有确定长期目标、实现这些目标的战略以及衡量进展的指标，国防部无法确定其行动是否能够解决弹药短缺问题。”包括国防部长皮特·赫格塞斯在内的高级政府官员否认美国存在弹药短缺，尽管有报告和独立分析显示，伊朗冲突已经严重耗尽了弹药。关键武器，特别是备受追捧的爱国者拦截机，其制造时间可能超过两年。
但在对政府问责局研究的回应中，五角大楼官员同意军方需要制定一项长期计划来提高弹药生产的建议。五角大楼负责采购的代理副手大卫·卡德曼写道：“我们同意需要一个总体框架，更好地整合弹药需求、库存水平、生产、资源和长期目标。”他补充说，国防部“已经执行了政府问责局建议中的许多内容”。美国政府问责局的研究并未探讨特定弹药的库存，而是研究了五角大楼跟踪、预测和总体处理一系列武器（从炮弹到战斧导弹）的过程。 “重要的是，[这项研究]与当前的短缺无关，”战略与国际研究中心的高级顾问马克·坎西恩（Mark Cancian）撰写了大量有关弹药政策的文章。 “这关系到未来并决定长期库存、生产和弹药组合。”  国防官员强调需要“高低”弹药组合，即高科技、难以制造的武器和廉价武器之间的平衡。伊朗战争说明了美军对昂贵拦截机的依赖，这些拦截机投入了大量资金来击落廉价的沙赫德无人机，这些无人机的成本只有数万美元。
彭博资讯国防分析师韦恩·桑德斯表示：“当你拥有先进的能力，并且开始消耗先进的能力来击落快速补充的非先进能力时，这是一场我们赢不了的经济游戏。”“这开始转变为军事领域的一场革命，表明我们必须改变我们的学说，同时改变我们在美国的生产能力。”   美国政府问责局国防能力主管戴安娜·摩尔达夫斯基 (Diana Moldafsky) 在周五发给《防务一号》的一封电子邮件中指出，五角大楼已经发现了不足之处

【原文 English Original】
The Defense Department has no “overarching plan” to identify, achieve, or measure its progress toward long-term munition production goals, according to a Government Accountability Office study released on Thursday, which said the military was too reactive to global events and unprepared to forecast its own needs. The GAO cited—among other issues—a lack of centralized authority over weapons inventories, which have been depleted by the Iran war and are vital to U.S. plans for a potential conflict with China. At the center of the problem lies a discrepancy between what the military can buy and what it actually needs, which the GAO said could even result in munition investments that exceed the Pentagon’s requirements.  “While DOD is taking steps to focus on munitions shortages, it is not positioned to address these gaps,” the report’s authors wrote. “DOD does not have an overarching plan or designated and empowered leadership to improve munition inventories and meet its munitions requirements. By not identifying long-term goals, strategies to achieve them, and metrics to gauge progress, DOD cannot be sure that its actions will address its munition shortfalls. ” Top administration officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have denied that the U.S. has a shortage in munitions, despite reports and independent analyses showing the Iran conflict has alarmingly drained key weapons, especially for highly-sought Patriot interceptors that can take more than two years to make. But in its response to the GAO study, Pentagon officials concurred with the recommendation that the military needed to develop a long-term plan to improve its munition production.  “We agree with the need for an overarching framework that better integrates munition requirements, inventory levels, production, resources, and long-term objectives,” wrote David Cadman, the Pentagon’s acting deputy for acquisitions, who added that the department “already executes many elements” of the GAO’s recommendation. The GAO study did not explore the inventories of specific munitions, but examined the processes by which an expansive list of weapons — from artillery shells to Tomahawk missiles — are tracked, forecast and generally addressed by the Pentagon. “The important thing is that [the study] is not about current shortages,” Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the Center for Strategic and International Studies who has written extensively on munitions policy. “It's about the future and deciding long-term inventories, production, and munitions mixes.”  Defense officials have emphasized the need for a “high-low” mix of munitions—that is, a balance between high-tech, hard-to-make weapons and cheaper ones. The Iran war illustrated the U.S. military’s reliance on expensive interceptors, which were heavily expended to shoot down cheap Shahed drones that only cost tens of thousands of dollars.  “When you have an exquisite capacity, and you are starting to expend an exquisite capacity to knock down non-exquisite capabilities that are rapidly replenished, it is an economical game that we're not going to win,” said Wayne Sanders, a defense analyst with Bloomberg Intelligence. “This is starting to turn into one of those revolutions in military affairs to say we have to change our doctrine as well as we change our production capacity in the U.S.”   In an email to Defense One on Friday, the GAO’s director for defense capabilities, Diana Moldafsky, noted that the Pentagon had identified shortfalls before the conflict with Iran, but said that the war “made addressing those shortages more urgent.” “Our key point is that meeting DOD's munitions requirements will be challenging,” Moldafsky said. “A department-wide plan would help the department direct its resources towards its most critical munitions needs.”  Cancian said that Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the consequent transfer of Patriots and other weapons to Kyiv, introduced concerns about the defense industrial base and its ability to respond to munition needs around the world. Meanwhile, the Pentagon has inked billions of dollars in multi-year “framework agreements” with top defense companies over the last year to help increase high-tech munition production, which require funding from Congress to come to fruition. The Trump administration also invoked the Defense Production Act earlier this year in an attempt to bolster munition supply chains. A Pentagon spokesperson declined to address the GAO study directly, or even to be quoted by name. But they said the military is “fully equipped to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing…while preserving a deep, ready stockpile to defend our people and interests.” Part of the problem is that no one authority is really in charge of keeping arsenals topped off and ready, the report found.  The GAO identified several Pentagon offices and working groups, including individual service entities, responsible for managing munition inventories, but no one dedicated authority “that empowers the leadership to make decisions that improve munitions inventories department-wide and hold them accountable for the outcomes achieved, such as improving munitions inventory levels.” The study also said that the services maintain separate tools to track munition inventories, which then feed into a Pentagon system known as the Munitions Readiness Initiative. But researchers said the DOD has limited oversight over that tracking platform and hasn’t regularly reconciled it with service-level numbers. Citing an unnamed Pentagon official in its acquisitions and sustainment office, the GAO said “the office was reluctant to impose additional responsibilities on the services for maintaining data to meet MRI’s needs because they recognize that the services already face numerous responsibilities in managing their own munitions inventory data.” The Pentagon concurred with most of the GAO’s recommendations, but only partially agreed with one: that the data management plan be run out of the DOD’s digital and AI office. Cadman’s response said that the Pentagon’s acquisition and sustainment arm was best suited to develop it. ]]>

title: China’s Naval Developments Set For The Spotlight At Zhuhai Airshow
zh_title: 中国海军发展成为珠海航展的焦点
summary: 中国人民解放军海军表示，正在准备在即将于珠海举行的第十六届中国国际航空航天博览会上进行重要亮相，军舰、舰载机、先进武器系统和无人平台将成为重点展示。扩大后的海军部分将包括在海湾另一边的高栏港设立一个新的海事装备展区，这标志着解放军海军首次在此次活动中设立这样的专门展示区。珠海已成为国际防务、航空领域最重要的赛事之一
content:
中国人民解放军海军表示，正在准备在即将于珠海举行的第十六届中国国际航空航天博览会上进行重要亮相，军舰、舰载机、先进武器系统和无人平台将成为重点展示。扩大后的海军部分将包括在海湾另一边的高栏港设立一个新的海事装备展区，这标志着解放军海军首次在此次活动中设立这样的专门展示区。珠海已成为国际国防和航空航天史上最重要的活动之一，成为中国快速发展的航空和军事工业的主要公开展示地。两年一度的中国国际航空航天展览会（俗称中国航展）于 1996 年首次举办，为展示中国一些最先进的军事硬件提供了难得的机会，其中包括在其他地方很少如此详细展示的飞机和系统。虽然该活动也是中国航空航天工业向潜在国际客户推广其产品的主要平台，但它日益成为展示新军事能力和提供难以评估的项目的重要场所。
第十五届中国国际航空航天展览会（又称 2024 年中国航展）于 2024 年 11 月 15 日在中国广东省珠海市中国国际航空航天展览中心举行。摄影：VCG/VCG via Getty Images 前几届已经取得了一些特别重大的进展。 2016 年的展会上，J-20 隐形战斗机首次公开飞行亮相，而 2018 年的展会则以不同寻常的方式展示了这架飞机，包括展示其装载空对空导弹的内部武器舱。 2022年的展会上，歼20首次在珠海进行静态展示，同时还有运20重型运输机、直20直升机以及在展会上进行首次飞行演示的运20空中加油机。最近，2024 年的展会特别引人注目的是 J-35A 隐形战斗机的公开亮相和具有弹射能力的 J-15T 舰​​载战斗机的出现。一架 J-15T 舰​​载战斗机在 2024 年中国航展上进行飞行表演。CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images 今年的展览定于 12 月 7 日至 13 日举行，除其他外，将展示中国海军的广泛能力，特别强调其舰载航空能力的快速发展，这一点我们过去已经详细讨论过。
预计将亮相的最引人注目的飞机包括 J-15T 舰载战斗机、作战型 J-35 隐形战斗机、KJ-600 舰载机载预警和控制 (AEW&C) 飞机、Z-20 直升机的几种海军型号，也许最重要的是新型 JL-15 舰载教练机，它是陆基 JL-10 的发展型。JL-15 舰载教练机的照片突出显示了制动钩和弹射器发射杆。虽然我们之前在珠海见过 J-15T，但如果它配备国产 WS-10H2 发动机，将会引起特别的兴趣。这样的配置将让人们更仔细地了解中国舰载侧卫衍生舰的最新演变

【原文 English Original】
China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) says it’s preparing a major presence at the upcoming 16th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai, with warships , carrier-based aircraft , advanced weapons systems, and uncrewed platforms set to feature prominently. The expanded naval component will include a new maritime equipment exhibition area at Gaolan Port, located just on the other side of the bay, marking the first time the PLAN has established such a dedicated display at the event. Zhuhai has become one of the most important events on the international defence and aerospace calendar, serving as China’s principal public showcase for its rapidly developing aviation and military industries. First held in 1996, the biennial China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, commonly known as Airshow China, provides an unusual opportunity to see some of the country’s most advanced military hardware, including aircraft and systems that are rarely shown in such detail elsewhere. While the event also serves as a major platform for China’s aerospace industry to promote its products to potential international customers , it has increasingly become an important venue for revealing new military capabilities and offering glimpses of programs that are otherwise difficult to assess. A general view of the 15th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, or Airshow China 2024, at the China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition Center on November 15, 2024, in Zhuhai, Guangdong Province of China. Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images Previous editions have produced some particularly significant developments. The 2016 show saw the J-20 stealth fighter make its first public flying appearance , while the 2018 edition provided an unusually revealing look at the aircraft, including a demonstration of its internal weapons bays, loaded with air-to-air missiles . The 2022 exhibition featured the J-20 on static display for the first time at Zhuhai, alongside the Y-20 heavy transport aircraft, Z-20 helicopter, and YY-20 aerial refueling tanker, which made its first flying demonstration at the event. More recently, the 2024 exhibition was particularly notable for the public debut of the J-35A stealth fighter and the appearance of the catapult-capable J-15T carrier-based fighter. A J-15T carrier-based fighter conducts a flight demonstration at Airshow China 2024. CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images This year’s exhibition, scheduled to take place from December 7 to 13, will showcase, among others, a broad range of the PLAN’s capabilities, with a particularly notable emphasis on the rapid evolution of its carrier aviation capabilities, something we have addressed in detail in the past . Among the most noteworthy aircraft expected to feature are the J-15T carrier-based fighter, the operational J-35 stealth fighter, the KJ-600 carrier-based airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft, several naval variants of the Z-20 helicopter, and, perhaps most significantly, the new JL-15 carrier-capable trainer, a development of the land-based JL-10 . A photo of the JL-15 carrier-capable trainer with the arrestor hook and catapult launch bar highlighted. Chinese internet via X While we have seen the J-15T at Zhuhai before, the aircraft will be of particular interest if it is shown with the indigenous WS-10H2 engine. Such a configuration would offer a closer look at the latest evolution of China’s carrier-based Flanker derivative and its ongoing transition toward a more domestically supported carrier aviation ecosystem. The appearance of the J-35 would be another major highlight. The aircraft represents a significant step in the PLAN’s carrier aviation ambitions, bringing a fifth-generation stealth fighter capability into the carrier air wing. Its presence would provide another opportunity to examine the progress of China’s next-generation naval fighter program. Back in 2014, Zhuhai saw the public debut of the FC-31 fighter demonstrator. At the time, it was still a land-based concept, and export was the main talking point, although there was already speculation about a naval variant, today’s J-35. A People’s Liberation Army Navy J-35 fighter during trials from the carrier Fujian last year. Chinese internet via X Meanwhile, the KJ-600 is arguably one of the most important developments in the PLAN’s carrier aviation ecosystem. The twin-engine turboprop aircraft is designed to provide airborne early warning and battle management capabilities, something that would transform the situational awareness and coordination available to China’s carrier strike groups. One of the first high-definition photos of the KJ-600 carrier-based airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft. Chinese internet via X Several variants of the Z-20 family are also expected to feature, reflecting the growing importance of helicopters in carrier operations, including airborne anti-submarine warfare, utility, and other maritime support missions. You can read more about the Z-20 family and other Chinese rotary-wing developments in this previous TWZ deep-dive on the topic . A Z-20F, the anti-submarine warfare variant of the naval Z-20 family. Three more naval Z-20s are seen in the hangar behind, including a Z-20J shipborne transport and assault variant. Chinese internet via X Perhaps the most intriguing aircraft on the list, however, is the JL-15. The JL-15 is derived from the Hongdu JL-10, also exported as the L-15 Falcon, a twin-engine advanced jet trainer and lead-in fighter trainer. The navalized development was initially reported to be designated JL-10J, but is now confirmed as being the JL-15. A tailhook-equipped mockup was spotted alongside the aircraft carrier Fujian in 2024. However, its operational status remains unclear, and China is known to have encountered difficulties with its earlier JL-9G naval trainer, whose tailhook was reportedly deleted following structural problems. Regarding the rumoured JL-10J carrier-capable jet trainer, another hint was spotted next to the carrier Fujian: It appears to be an unfinished JL-10J mockup stored on the dockside . So question is: Two tails as shown in the latest CG or just one like the regular JL-10? pic.twitter.com/BM8W8MRGWK — @Rupprecht_A (@RupprechtDeino) March 19, 2024 Its appearance would provide a particularly interesting indication of how China is thinking about training its next generation of carrier-based pilots. A carrier-capable development of the JL-10 would be an important addition to the emerging carrier aviation ecosystem, bridging the gap between conventional jet training and the demanding requirements of operating from an aircraft carrier. The JL-15 also makes an interesting comparison with the U.S. Navy’s somewhat stuttering efforts to introduce a new training jet for its carrier pilots. The U.S. Navy’s Undergraduate Jet Training System (UJTS) program is intended to replace its aging fleet of T-45 Goshawk trainers, but the acquisition effort has encountered considerable difficulties. Earlier this month, we described how Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) withdrew its proposed clean-sheet Freedom Jet from the competition, citing concerns over the Navy’s insistence on firm-fixed-price production commitments before the aircraft’s design had sufficiently matured. This leaves the Beechcraft M-346N , based on Leonardo’s established M-346 Master , as the only publicly known remaining contender . The program has also experienced schedule slippage, with the initial contract award now expected in the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027. Perhaps more significant is the difference in the two services’ approaches to carrier aviation training. The U.S. Navy has removed the requirement for its next-generation jet trainer to be capable of operating from an actual aircraft carrier, including carrier qualification and simulated carrier touch-and-goes at land-based facilities. Instead, it increasingly relies on advanced simulation, virtualized training, and assisted carrier landing technologies to prepare pilots for the demands of carrier operations. The JL-15, by contrast, is intended to support carrier-based pilot training. A dedicated carrier-capable trainer could offer China a more direct pathway for preparing pilots for operations aboard its increasingly sophisticated — and expanding — carrier fleet. Taken together, the PLAN aircraft being lined up for Zhuhai this year illustrate the increasingly sophisticated and integrated nature of China’s carrier aviation ambitions . As well as the aircraft carriers and their embarked aircraft, these ambitions also require other surface and subsurface vessels to operate effectively. Uncrewed systems will form another important part of the display. The exhibition will include aerial drones, uncrewed underwater vehicles, and other autonomous platforms, reflecting the PLAN’s growing interest in the potential of uncrewed warfare. Chinese media reports suggest that the WZ-2 uncrewed helicopter will receive its public debut at Zhuhai, while the PLAN may well also want to capitalize on its recent announcement that it had successfully launched and recovered a GJ-21 stealthy flying-wing uncrewed combat air vehicle (UCAV) aboard the Type 076 amphibious assault ship Sichuan . GJ-21. Chinese internet via X A chance to see the GJ-21 up close would be a huge deal, but there are many other naval drone options that could be revealed in more detail. There are likely to be more navalized collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) concepts and developments, especially since the adoption of the electromagnetic aircraft launch system (EMALS) catapult opens up a huge range of possibilities for uncrewed aircraft operating as part of a carrier air wing. Potentially, these could include the mysterious MQ-25-like drone that we recently discussed , the role of which remains unclear. On top of that, constant CCA testing at locations such as Malan suggests there could be much more to discuss than just the systems officially highlighted. Many other naval drones will surely be on display as well, including lower-end attritable concepts. Beyond static displays, China’s navy plans to organize flight demonstrations, formation flights, and simulated operational exercises. Its stated aim is to highlight not only the capabilities of individual platforms but also their ability to operate together in complex maritime environments. Photos have emerged showing apparent rehearsals for the display, presenting examples of the J-15, J-35, and KJ-600 to represent Beijing’s broader carrier air wing ecosystem. Two J-15s, two J-35s, and a KJ-600 purportedly taking part in a rehearsal for a formation fly-over at Zhuhai. Chinese internet via X It is not immediately clear which versions of the J-15 are participating in this formation flight: they could be J-15Ts, but another possibility is the electronic warfare version, the J-15DT , that we have profiled in the past. Regardless, they highlight how China’s carrier aviation ambitions are increasingly focused on catapult-assisted takeoff but arrested recovery (CATOBAR) operations, which offer many advantages . The J-15DT electronic warfare version of the Chinese carrier Flanker is outfitted for operations aboard catapult-equipped flattops like the Fujian . Chinese internet via X For the first time, the exhibition will also include a substantial surface fleet component, making use of the docks at the nearby Gaolan Port. Among the vessels expected to be featured are the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, the Type 055 guided-missile destroyer, and the Type 054A guided-missile frigate. Their presence will offer a public-facing showcase of China’s increasingly sophisticated surface fleet and its expanding range of maritime capabilities. It should also be recalled that it was at Gaolan Port where at least one Chinese uncrewed surface vessel , a distinctive trimaran craft, was first spotted. The Type 055 guided-missile destroyer Nanchang sails during the naval exercise Joint Sea-2021 on October 19, 2021, in the Western part of the Pacific Ocean. Photo by Sun Zifa/China News Service via Getty Images The broader messaging surrounding the exhibition is also notable. According to the PLAN, this year’s displays will place greater emphasis on operational readiness and training, with active-duty equipment that regularly participates in exercises and maritime security missions taking precedence over purely exhibition-oriented displays. This should underscore how Beijing has rapidly spun up its naval capabilities, introducing new and more capable equipment that is increasingly capable of more sustained out-of-area operations. The expanded naval presence at Zhuhai looks set to provide a substantial public showcase of China’s ongoing naval modernization. As well as the combination of the J-15T, J-35, KJ-600, and Z-20 variants, the JL-15 points to an increasingly comprehensive carrier aviation enterprise. And, judging by previous editions of the show, there will almost certainly be more novelties on display as well. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post China’s Naval Developments Set For The Spotlight At Zhuhai Airshow appeared first on TWZ .

title: Dispatch from 2032: After Chinese salvos fail to defeat Taiwan, Beijing is trapped in a war of attrition
zh_title: 2032年快讯：中国联军未能击败台湾，北京陷入消耗战
summary: 2032 年快讯：中国齐射未能击败台湾后，北京陷入消耗战 - 大西洋理事会的军舰和中国人民解放军 (PLA) 海军战斗机于 2018 年 4 月 12 日在南海参加军事展示。（路透社/斯金格，来自Reuters Connect）本文是斯考克罗夫特中心的系列文章“来自下一场战争的快讯”的一部分印度-太平洋安全倡议，其中我们的专家对世界下一场重大冲突在最有可能爆发的地区可能会是什么样子进行了假设：
content:
2032年快讯：中国的齐射未能击败台湾，北京陷入消耗战 - 大西洋理事会
2018 年 4 月 12 日，中国人民解放军 (PLA) 海军的军舰和战斗机参加在南海举行的军事展示。（路透社/斯金格，来自Reuters Connect）
本文是斯考克罗夫特中心印度-太平洋安全倡议系列“下一场战争的快报”的一部分，其中我们的专家对世界下一场重大冲突可能在最有可能爆发的地区印度-太平洋地区进行了假设。这些消息被称为虚构情报，或“FicInt”，在军队内部使用，让政策制定者为可能的未来做好准备。目的是防止下一场战争爆发。
2032 年，台北——中国第一批导弹和无人机在夜深人静时飞越台湾海峡。有些在咆哮的火焰喷射的推动下划过黑色的天空，而另一些则安静地、几乎看不见地以稳定的速度在黑暗的天空中嗡嗡作响。第一个被拦截导弹击中中国火柱摧毁，其他则在被激光闪光击中时爆炸。有些被小型拦截无人机撞到一边。一些人被自动炮和机枪的火幕击落，曳光弹在黑暗中摸索着目标，越来越多的条纹。
这些联合火力打击——中国对台战争中所宣称的第一次攻击——旨在摧毁台湾的防御，使其军事力量丧失能力，并粉碎台湾人的战斗意志。尽管这些齐射令人恐惧且令人印象深刻，但它们未能实现中国的目标。
一些袭击成功了，坠入港口、机场和军事基地，并向天空喷出滚滚火焰和浓烟。北至台北，南至高雄，台湾一次又一次遭到无情的打击。虽然台湾军事力量的来源是中国的目标，但许多平民也因这次袭击而被屠杀。世界领导人最初等着看台湾是否能够承受住这场冲击，或者是否会像许多分析人士预测的那样迅速崩溃。
但事实证明，台湾的多层防空和导弹防御系统“T-Dome”出乎意料地有效。尽管该公司在 2027 年首次投入运营时（即 2025 年宣布成立两年后）面临性能困难，但其许多自主系统的可靠性迅速成熟。随着中国入侵台湾领空和侵略性海上骚扰的行为年复一年变得更加频繁和充满敌意，台湾的总统和指挥官们更加放心地相信T-Dome允许自主攻击其认定的敌对目标。
尽管中国在发动袭击之前发起了旨在破坏台湾指挥和控制系统的强大网络攻势，但台湾慷慨地使用了 Anthropic 的 Claude Mythos 等前沿人工智能 (AI) 网络安全模型，发现并修补了几乎所有潜在的攻击向量，从而保持了 T-Dome 和其他系统的运行。对人工智能抱有如此大的信心的争议是不可避免的。战时的防御效果则不然。
T-Dome 证明了这些高风险决策的正确性，在第一轮攻击中拦截了 90% 的中国弹药。这为台湾指挥官赢得了宝贵的时间来分散兵力，使中国更难瞄准他们，采取预先计划

Dispatch from 2032: After Chinese salvos fail to defeat Taiwan, Beijing is trapped in a war of attrition - Atlantic Council
Warships and fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy take part in a military display in the South China Sea on April 12, 2018. (REUTERS/Stringer via Reuters Connect)
This article is part of “Dispatches from the Next War,” a series from the Scowcroft Center’s Indo-Pacific Security Initiative in which our experts provide hypothetical accounts of what the world’s next major conflict could look like in the region where it’s most likely to break out: the Indo-Pacific. These dispatches are styled as fictional intelligence, or “FicInt,” which is used within the military to prepare policymakers for possible futures. The aim is to prevent the next war from ever unfolding.
TAIPEI, 2032—China’s first missiles and drones flew across the Taiwan Strait in the dead of night. Some coursed across the black sky propelled by growling jets of flame, while others quietly and near-invisibly hummed through the dark sky at a steady pace. The first were destroyed by interceptor missiles snaking into Chinese columns of fire, others exploded when hit by flashes of laser light. Some were knocked aside by tiny interceptor drones. A few were downed by curtains of autocannon and machine-gun fire, with the growing streaks of tracer bullets groping for targets in the dark.
These joint firepower strikes—the vaunted first attack of China’s war on Taiwan—were meant to smash Taiwan’s defenses, incapacitate its military force, and shatter the Taiwanese will to fight. While these salvoes were terrifying and impressive, they failed to achieve China’s objectives.
Some of the attacks got through, crashing into ports, airfields, and military bases, and sending plumes of flame and smoke into the sky. From Taipei in the north to Kaohsiung in the south, Taiwan was mercilessly hit again and again. While sources of Taiwanese military power were China’s target, many civilians were also slaughtered by the attack. World leaders initially waited to see whether Taiwan could withstand the onslaught or whether it would quickly fold as many analysts had predicted.
But the T-Dome, Taiwan’s multi-layered air- and missile-defense system, proved unexpectedly effective. While it faced performance difficulties when it first became operational in 2027, two years after its announcement in 2025, the reliability of many of its autonomous systems matured rapidly. As China’s incursions into Taiwan’s airspace and aggressive maritime harassment grew more frequent and hostile year after year, Taiwan’s presidents and commanders became more comfortable putting greater faith in the T-Dome’s permission to autonomously engage targets it identified as hostile.
And while China’s strikes were preceded by a robust cyber offensive aimed at disrupting Taiwan’s command-and-control systems, Taiwan’s generous use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) cybersecurity models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos had discovered and patched nearly every potential attack vector, keeping the T-Dome and other systems operational. The controversy about placing so much faith in AI was inevitable; the defensive results in wartime were not.
The T-Dome vindicated those high-risk decisions, intercepting 90 percent of Chinese munitions in the first barrage. This bought Taiwan’s commanders precious time to disperse their forces and make it more difficult for China to target them, take up preplanned fighting positions across their nation, and start fighting back.
Further, the survivability and resilience of many Taiwanese bases, stations, and command posts proved to be highly robust. Many were built underground and were well-protected by dozens of meters of earth and rock. Missile after missile and drone after drone slammed into the vicinity of these underground command posts. While some were disrupted, as antennas were toppled and wiring cut, most remained operational.
Notably, Taiwan’s air force was able to maintain aviation command and control from its underground airbase within Toad Mountain, contributing both to air defense and strike missions of its own. Above-ground targets in Taiwan, such as airfields and main supply routes, were initially cratered and some aircraft were destroyed. But Taiwanese engineers repaired airfields, roads, and bases with alacrity. As a result, such hits resulted only in temporary pauses in Taiwan’s operations and did not amount to debilitating knock-out blows.
With most of its forces intact, Taiwan counter-attacked, firing its own munitions at key targets across mainland China. Many of these were intercepted. But due to the superior quality and reliability of Taiwan’s munitions, and China’s years-long strategic emphasis on offensive rather than defensive capabilities, a disproportionate number of Taiwanese munitions hit their marks.
In addition, the United States, Japan, and other nations provided Taiwan with exquisite intelligence and provided non-attributable, non-kinetic cyber and space capabilities that greatly enhanced the hit-rate of Taiwan’s defensive counterstrikes. Consequently, Taiwan devastated targets such as the ports where China’s amphibious forces were assembling, crippling the invasion before it even got underway. Chinese aviation command-and-control nodes and over-the-horizon radars were also hammered, giving Taiwan’s air force greater freedom of maneuver than most analysts had ever predicted.
The effects on Taiwanese morale were immeasurable. As with the US military’s famous Doolittle Raid on Japan after Pearl Harbor, the physical damage Taiwan inflicted on China was less important than the political and psychological results of Taiwan’s demonstrated resilience. Taiwan was not helpless, and the People’s Republic of China was not an invincible juggernaut.
With the quick, decisive campaign China had envisioned to isolate and invade Taiwan thwarted, the joint firepower strikes pressed on. Days dragged into weeks. Taiwan began running dry on interceptors, cannons began to jam, and even lasers began to burn out. Taiwan was forced to absorb more direct hits from Chinese strikes, even as China’s own magazines ran low.
If the war were evaluated today based on targets hit, the assessment would find that China has a commanding lead. But even with Taiwan’s dwindling munitions, the forces still in the fight have proven disproportionately effective. As the United States painfully experienced during Operation Epic Fury in Iran, even a greatly diminished adversary can still hold the advantage if it fights asymmetrically and selectively. While short on missiles, Taiwan has maintained plenty of launchers and conducted carefully sequenced strikes layered with joint operations and allied intelligence support that continue to bloody China’s nose. China’s Eastern Theater Command has still refused to launch an invasion fleet across the strait, as the mere preservation of Taiwan’s stand-in forces held the amphibious force at risk, making the amphibious invasion appear infeasible.
China—and the world—also grossly underestimated Taiwanese resolve. Despite polling that showed Taiwanese willingness to fight as even higher than that of Ukrainians prior to the Russian invasion in 2022, many analysts were skeptical that Taiwan would hold fast under the pressure of a Chinese offensive. Such analysts had focused primarily on the correlation of forces and means between China and Taiwan, weighing their assessments on numeric comparisons of ships, jets, and missiles available to both sides. This, however, failed to account for qualitative differences in Chinese and Taiwanese systems and societies, or for fundamental human elements that have always characterized the conduct of war. While bombing alone was not China’s plan, China had been as yet unable to launch its amphibious invasion because it could not set the necessary conditions. Bombing alone has never produced capitulation, and it has not here in Taipei.
Moreover, China’s narrative warfare and United Front activities, its strategic co-opting of domestic groups, had also penetrated swaths of Taiwanese society and foreign discourse, influencing pre-war public commentary to give a dim view of Taiwanese will and an overinflated view of Chinese prowess. The extreme pro-unification wing of the Kuomintang, the Chinese Nationalist Party in Taiwan, aligned itself with Beijing before the war. A few American commentators had advocated strategic restraint, isolationism, and nativism, while some American politicians echoed these sentiments, leading many to presume Taiwan would surrender at the first blush with its enemy.
But as with the staunch resolve of Ukrainians, it appears the Taiwanese are prepared to fight for years if necessary to preserve the democracy and way of life they built after ending martial law in 1987. Under attack, as they have seen their people killed in the streets, the Taiwanese have bravely rallied, pro-unification extremists have been politically isolated, and public sentiment in favor of taidu, formal Taiwanese independence, has skyrocketed. Civil-defense initiatives and energy-diversification efforts, which had been maturing for years, have also mentally prepared the population and the entire society to be resilient despite the immediate imposition of incredible hardship across the country.
Beijing now faces a dilemma. Backing down could deal a fatal blow to the credibility of the Chinese Communist Party, while pressing on would mean doubling down on sunk costs and putting the government’s dream of national rejuvenation further out of reach. Caught in a trap of its own making, China has looked abroad to Russia and North Korea for other solutions, while the Central Military Commission has begun to consider limited nuclear strikes to turn the tide in China’s favor.
Magazine depth cuts both ways. Taiwan may run low on munitions first in a future conflict, but even Chinese inventories are not limitless. And because China cannot hit everything at once, it will likely have to focus on high-priority targets, yielding maneuver space for Taiwanese forces.
Range rings also cut both ways. Taiwan falls within the range of most Chinese strike capabilities. China, too, is within range of many of Taiwan’s strike capabilities. If Taiwan is attacked by China, Taiwan will strike back at targets in China—not just at munitions or forces entering Taiwanese territory.
The earth is the most reliable and affordable shield. Interceptors are necessary, but they can be expensive and can quickly run dry under constant barrage. While difficult to scale, subterranean fortifications reduce reliance on interceptors and mitigate China’s ability to effectively target Taiwan’s forces.
Regardless of when, why, and how China may start the fight, the result would likely be a protracted war with Taiwan. Beijing may intend—and pundits may predict—a quick surrender by Taipei, but this is unlikely. There are many “roads to war” and rationales Beijing will claim led to its aggression, and many ways the war might begin, including a quarantine, a blockade, or outright attack. Regardless, China is unlikely to win rapidly or easily, almost inevitably leading to a protracted and costly conflict—if Taiwan continues its defense and resilience efforts.
Even successful strikes rarely deliver knockout blows, and an active defense can prove resilient even under sustained strike campaigns. Defenders will disperse to preserve forces and capabilities, and can rapidly repair airfields, ports, and bases.
When nations are attacked, cohesion surges, even among politically divided states. Blood calls for blood, defenders rally to their flag, and the will to fight becomes stronger than ever.
Third parties are not easily intimidated into total non-participation in wars that impact them. When nations can pursue their interests and frustrate their adversaries at low risk, they will.

content:
香港宏福苑大火一周年，BBC中文專訪多位遇難者家屬，紀錄他們災後如何走過一年。2025年11月26日，大埔宏福苑發生香港數十年以最致命火災，奪去168條性命，1984戶失去家園。
「11月26號之後，這條刺永遠都在我心內，可能直到我躺在棺材仍在，不會消散、不會磨滅。」
Christy全家居於最先起火的宏昌閣，她的丈夫逃生時在樓梯間遇難，當時一對子女年僅9歲和6歲。直至現在，她仍然經常拿起手機向丈夫昔日的電話號碼發短訊聊表思念。身為社工的她確診創傷後遺症與抑鬱症，努力適應成為家中唯一支柱的新生活。
火災後，蘇氏夫婦經常到墳場為年逾80歲的父母洗擦合葬墓地，相鄰一片都是新造的墓碑，全部刻著「終於二零二五年十一月廿六日」，屬於一同罹難的宏福苑街坊。媽媽的遺體最後只剩下一個飯盒大小的骸骨，蘇先生在燒成灰燼的舊居尋回雙親遺物，爸爸的手錶在烈焰下永遠定格。他和太太居於另一座的物業沒被大火波及，但政府決定一併收回拆卸，兩人仍未安頓長遠安置。
過去一年，遺屬在等一份調查報告，在排期申請法律援助，在學習如何向年幼的孩子解釋死亡。大火後11個月，香港政府公布獨立委員會調查報告點名四個部門有缺失，特首率官員鞠躬道歉，局長引咎辭職，數十人被捕或起訴。但對許多家庭來說，他們仍在傷痛中等待漫長的司法程序，部分人正申請法援計劃追討傷亡賠償。

title: Huang is back at Nvidia. But the fight over who controls chip exports is just beginning.
zh_title: 黄回到了英伟达。但谁控制芯片出口的斗争才刚刚开始。
summary: 黄回到了英伟达。但谁控制芯片出口的斗争才刚刚开始。 - 大西洋理事会 Nvidia 首席执行官黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 于 2026 年 6 月 1 日在台湾台北举行的年度电脑展期间发表主题演讲，在主题演讲中介绍了 RTX Spark GPU。（路透社/Ann Wang/档案照片）华盛顿——在数周有关涉嫌间谍、秘密事务和涉嫌芯片转移的报道并最终导致他于 11 月 12 日辞职后，黄仁勋重新执掌 Nvidia。在美国总统唐纳德·特朗普呼吁采取行动后，该公司董事会昨天恢复了他的首席执行官兼总裁职务。
content:
黄回到了英伟达。但谁控制芯片出口的斗争才刚刚开始。 - 大西洋理事会
Nvidia 首席执行官黄仁勋于 2026 年 6 月 1 日在台湾台北举行的年度电脑展期间发表主题演讲，介绍了 RTX Spark GPU。（路透社/Ann Wang/档案照片）
华盛顿——数周以来，关于涉嫌间谍、秘密事务和涉嫌芯片转移的报道最终导致黄仁勋于 11 月 12 日辞职，黄仁勋重新执掌 Nvidia。昨天，在美国总统唐纳德·特朗普召开董事会会议后，该公司董事会恢复了他的首席执行官兼总裁职务，亲自敦促董事会成员让他回归，并向他们保证他的回归不会构成国家安全风险。尽管市场对黄的回归反应积极，但促使他离开的担忧并未消失。关于英伟达在涉嫌将芯片转移到中国的事件中所扮演的角色以及更广泛的华盛顿应如何限制中国获得先进计算的问题仍然存在。
但黄的回归之际，华盛顿的政治势头已经转向收紧出口管制。黄仁勋是呼吁放宽对中国高端芯片销售限制的最知名人士之一，他认为这些限制将促使北京开发国内替代品。然而，这一丑闻促使人们呼吁打击对中国的芯片出口。在国会，两党都支持加强审查和额外立法，而特朗普政府部分人士则呼吁更严格地执行现有控制措施。黄的复职不太可能扭转这一趋势。然而，目前尚不清楚的是国会或政府是否会带头制定出口管制的新方针。
英伟达丑闻在政府内部引起了相当多的不和。据报道，美国官员怀疑中国情报部门在事件曝光前几个月就锁定了黄。 11月13日，美国财政部长斯科特·贝森特表示，财政部和其他机构几个月来一直在推动将涉嫌将英伟达先进芯片转移到中国的新加坡云计算公司Megaspeed添加到商务部的实体名单中，该名单是美国公司需要获得出口许可证的外国公司、组织和个人的贸易黑名单。商务部推迟了决定。本周早些时候，特朗普为黄做出担保，称“他没有做错任何事”，这一举动引起了两党的批评。
商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克受到了很多关注。据报道，他推迟了对涉嫌将芯片转移到中国的公司的打击行动，而特朗普在英伟达丑闻爆发之前和之后都授权了这一行动。据报道，在英伟达总法律顾问联系商务官员后，商务部还于 2025 年 8 月停止了对 Megaspeed 的调查，并最终将调查移交给司法部。此后，卢特尼克同意在国会作证，众议院民主党人已开始调查他的家族在英伟达的持股是否影响了他的决定。
迄今为止，政府最重要的一步是 11 月 16 日发布的一项关于远程访问先进芯片的新商务规则。新规则要求公司获得许可，在已知接收设施提供信号的情况下，将先进芯片转移到美国境外的任何数据中心。

【原文 English Original】
Huang is back at Nvidia. But the fight over who controls chip exports is just beginning. - Atlantic Council
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang introduces the RTX Spark GPU during a keynote address on the sidelines of the annual Computex in Taipei, Taiwan, on June 1, 2026. (REUTERS/Ann Wang/File Photo)
WASHINGTON—After weeks of reports about alleged spies, secret affairs, and suspected chip diversion that culminated in his resignation on November 12, Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated him as CEO and president yesterday, after US President Donald Trump called into a board meeting, personally urging board members to bring him back and assuring them that his return posed no national security risks. And while the markets reacted positively to Huang’s return, the concerns that prompted his departure have not gone away. Questions remain about the role Nvidia played in the suspected diversion of chips to China and, more broadly, about how Washington should curb Chinese access to advanced computing.
But Huang’s return comes while Washington’s political momentum is already shifting toward tighter export controls. Huang was one of the most prominent voices calling for looser restrictions on high-end chip sales to China, arguing that these restrictions would push Beijing to develop domestic alternatives. The scandal, however, has prompted calls for a crackdown on chip exports to China. On the Hill, there is bipartisan support for more scrutiny and additional legislation, while parts of the Trump administration have called for stricter enforcement of existing controls. Huang’s reinstatement is unlikely to reverse that course. What remains unclear, however, is whether Congress or the administration will take the lead in charting a new course for export controls.
The Nvidia scandal generated a fair amount of discord within the administration. US officials reportedly suspected that Chinese intelligence had targeted Huang months before the story broke. On November 13, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the Treasury Department and other agencies had pushed for months to add Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced chips to China, to the Commerce Department’s entity list, a trade blacklist of foreign companies, organizations, and individuals that US firms need a license to export. Commerce had delayed the decision. And earlier this week, Trump vouched for Huang, saying “he did nothing wrong”—a move that has drawn bipartisan criticism.
Much scrutiny has fallen on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He reportedly stalled implementation of a crackdown on companies suspected of diverting chips to China that Trump had authorized both before and after the Nvidia scandal broke. The Commerce Department also reportedly halted its inquiry into Megaspeed in August 2025, after Nvidia’s general counsel contacted Commerce officials, and ultimately handed the investigation over to the Justice Department. Lutnick has since agreed to testify before Congress, and House Democrats have opened an investigation into whether his family’s holdings in Nvidia shaped his decisions.
The administration’s most significant step so far is a new Commerce rule, published on November 16, on remote access to advanced chips. The new rule requires that companies acquire a license to transfer advanced chips to any data center outside the United States when the recipient facility is known to provide significant computing power to companies headquartered in China or other embargoed countries. It also includes license requirements to export advanced chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil.
The rule addresses an important loophole that Chinese companies have been using to access advanced US chips, but it has limits of its own. It works by regulating the physical chips rather than the provision of computing power itself, over which the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security lacks explicit authority to control. Its effectiveness also rests on firms knowing and reporting who uses their computing power. To make the rule work in practice, Commerce would need to issue the kind of detailed guidance the Treasury Department provides banks and firms when it imposes sanctions, including red flags, due diligence expectations, and answers to frequently asked questions. Notably, the rule was written “by and at the direction of” the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, according to Commerce, a highly unusual qualification and a likely indication of continuing disagreement within the administration.
Yesterday, after much internal pressure, Commerce also added Megaspeed and six affiliates to the entity list. In addition, the Justice Department is leading a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, and the Securities and Exchange Commission has opened its own investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices.
Taken together, these actions reveal a muddled approach to the problem. The administration has taken steps to strengthen export control enforcement, but at the same time, it is standing behind government officials who failed to prevent chip diversion, as well as the Nvidia executive at the center of the scandal. Its toughest measure came from Treasury and the National Security Council, rather than the department responsible for export controls. As long as disagreements within the administration delay enforcement and produce inconsistent licensing decisions, firms and allies will struggle to know where the lines are, and those seeking to divert chips will keep looking for gaps.
By contrast, the scandal has generated broad bipartisan support in Congress for stronger controls, and several bills already in circulation target the gaps it exposed. The Chip Security Act would require location verification for advanced AI chips before export, turning voluntary tools such as Nvidia’s opt-in tracking into a common standard. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Bureau of Industry and Security explicit authority to regulate remote access to controlled chips, filling the gap the new Commerce rule leaves. The AI OVERWATCH Act would give Congress thirty days to review, and potentially block, licenses for advanced chip exports to adversaries such as China. And the MATCH Act would press allies to align their controls on chipmaking equipment with those of the United States.
While these bills may have faced difficulty passing as stand-alone legislation, lawmakers are now seeking to include them in the fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which is expected to pass before the end of the year but has no fixed deadline. The Senate’s version already puts forward the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act for inclusion in the NDAA, and leaders in both parties have signaled support for keeping them in the final bill. This offers a more promising path to enactment and reduces the risk of a presidential veto. The NDAA has passed every year for more than six decades and vetoing it over export control provisions would be politically far more costly than blocking a single bill. It is more likely that the White House will play a role in shaping the final text in conference or retain flexibility in how rules are implemented.
However, not every bill faces the same odds. The Chip Security Act passed the House Foreign Affairs Committee unanimously, making it the most likely to clear. The MATCH Act, in contrast, likely faces more resistance because it reaches beyond US companies. If allies such as the Netherlands and Japan do not align their controls on chipmaking equipment, the Act would effectively extend US restrictions to their firms. That risks significant diplomatic friction, which Congress may seek to avoid. The Dutch government has also already lobbied against curbs targeting the sales of ASML, the Dutch manufacturer of machines used to make advanced chips. This suggests that if the MATCH Act survives, it may be in a narrower form.
Moving forward, Congress has the opportunity to play an important role in shaping US export controls. While the Commerce Department’s technical expertise in this space remains pivotal to a well-functioning export control regime, its decisions are only as durable as the priorities of the administration it serves. In recent years, rules have been drafted and withdrawn, licensing decisions have shifted with political priorities, and enforcement has stalled amid internal disputes. If Congress were to codify key controls, it would give firms and allies clearer and more durable rules that are harder to reverse or use as bargaining chips. Congress should also use the upcoming hearings with Lutnick and Huang to examine how licensing and enforcement decisions were made.
The next few months will show which way the balance tips. Negotiations over the NDAA in December will decide whether the chip bills become law, and the hearings with Lutnick and Huang will test how far Congress is willing to press the administration. In January, a Democratic-controlled Congress takes over, with Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) set to chair the Banking Committee, which would review chip export licenses if AI OVERWATCH passes. For Commerce, the test comes by mid-February, when the remote access rule’s grace period for existing data center operations ends. Whether it issues clear guidance and follows the Megaspeed listing with action against other suspected chip diverters will show whether enforcement is becoming a priority again.

content:
罗兴亚种族灭绝裁决面临地缘政治考验 - 大西洋理事会
2017 年 8 月 31 日，在孟加拉国特克纳夫，罗兴亚难民在非法越境后被孟加拉国边防卫队扣留，试图躲避暴雨。（路透社/Mohammad Ponir Hossain/档案照片）
康涅狄格州中城——11 月 19 日，国际法院 (ICJ) 裁定缅甸应对罗辛亚社区的种族灭绝负责。这是国际法院首次判定一个国家对种族灭绝负有责任。同日，美国总统特朗普、中国国家主席习近平和俄罗斯总统普京在深圳会晤后发表声明，警告国际刑事法院滥用管辖权。该声明提到了国际刑事法院和“其他类似机构”，其措辞广泛到足以涵盖联合国主要司法机构国际法院。第二天，缅甸总统发言人在一份声明中提到了三位领导人在国际法庭上的立场，认为国际法院的裁决“不公平”。这表明缅甸执行该判决中规定的措施，特别是对罗兴亚人获得公民身份的保护，可能取决于大国利益所影响的谈判。
这一判决的公民概念表明了真正的利害关系。国际法院承认，剥夺罗兴亚人公民身份是歧视框架的一部分，这与其种族灭绝意图的调查结果有关。尽管如此，它认为给予每个罗辛亚人充分和平等的公民身份“超出了防止另一场种族灭绝的适当保障的范围”。然而，国际法院确实下令采取赔偿措施，包括“确保保护罗兴亚人免受歧视和迫害”。判决书在两处指出，这项措施包括“在获得公民身份方面”和“在获得公民身份方面和在迁徙自由方面保护免受歧视”。
由于法院没有下令缅甸授予罗兴亚人公民身份，罗兴亚人是否真正获得公民身份将取决于在缅甸拥有利益的政府已经参与的政治谈判。从华盛顿对稀土的兴趣到北京的皎漂港口和新德里的加拉丹运输走廊，世界各国政府在就进入其领土和资源问题与缅甸政府进行谈判时，都面临着一个关键选择。他们可以将罗兴亚公民身份纳入政治安排，也可以接受罗兴亚人的持续排斥，以追求自己的战略利益。外部势力应该利用包括贸易在内的影响力，使裁决的实施以及早该实现的公民身份和安全返回之路成为他们支持的任何解决方案的一部分。
国际法院于 2026 年 11 月 19 日在荷兰海牙就指控缅甸对罗兴亚穆斯林少数民族进行种族灭绝的案件作出判决。（路透社/Piroschka van de Wouw）
如果外部势力支持一项让罗兴亚人成为无国籍人的解决方案，那么将他们赶出缅甸的条件将继续存在，而另一次外逃将变得更有可能。法官莱昂纳多·内梅尔·卡尔代拉·布兰特和专案法官纳维·皮莱在联合声明中指出，缅甸确保平等获得公民身份的义务应解读为：

【原文 English Original】
The Rohingya genocide ruling faces a geopolitical test - Atlantic Council
Rohingya refugees try to take shelter from torrential rain as they are held by the Border Guard Bangladesh after illegally crossing the border, in Teknaf, Bangladesh, on August 31, 2017. (REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain/File Photo)
MIDDLETOWN, Connecticut—On November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya community. It is the first time that the ICJ has held a state responsible for committing genocide. On the same day, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a declaration after their meeting in Shenzhen that warned against jurisdictional abuse by the International Criminal Court (ICC). The declaration named the ICC and “other similar bodies,” language broad enough to cover the ICJ, the UN’s principal judicial organ. The following day, the spokesperson of the Myanmar president referred to the stance of the three leaders on international courts during a statement that deemed the ICJ’s ruling “unfair.” This would suggest that Myanmar’s implementation of the measures ordered in this judgment, especially its protections on access to citizenship for the Rohingyas, could depend on negotiations shaped by the interests of great powers.
This judgment’s notion of citizenship shows what is really at stake. The ICJ recognized that the denial of citizenship to the Rohingya people was part of a framework of discrimination, which was relevant to its findings on genocidal intent. Nevertheless, it considered granting full and equal citizenship to every Rohingya as “beyond the scope” of appropriate guarantees against another genocide. However, the ICJ did order measures of restitution, including to “ensure the protection of the Rohingya from discrimination and persecution.” The judgment noted in two places that this measure includes “with respect to access to citizenship” and “protection from discrimination in accessing citizenship and with respect to freedom of movement.”
Because the court stopped short of ordering Myanmar to grant citizenship, whether the Rohingya actually receive it will depend on political negotiations in which governments with their own stakes in Myanmar are already engaged. Governments across the world that are in talks with the Myanmar government when it comes to getting access to its territory and resources, from Washington’s interest in rare earths to Beijing’s port at Kyaukphyu and New Delhi’s Kaladan transport corridor, face a crucial choice. They can integrate Rohingya citizenship into the political arrangement, or they can accept the Rohingya’s continued exclusion in order to pursue their own strategic interests. Outside powers should use their leverage, including trade, to make the ruling’s implementation and a long-overdue path to citizenship and safe return part of any settlement they support.
The ICJ delivers its judgment in the case accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority, in The Hague, Netherlands, on November 19, 2026. (REUTERS/Piroschka van de Wouw)
If outside powers back a settlement that leaves the Rohingya stateless, the conditions that drove them from Myanmar will remain, and another exodus will become more likely. In their joint declaration, Judge Leonardo Nemer Caldeira Brant and Judge ad hoc Navi Pillay noted that Myanmar’s obligation to ensure equal access to citizenship should be read into the operative part of the judgment. While recognizing that states have sovereign authority to decide citizenship requirements, they stressed that access to citizenship is necessary for protection and non-recurrence.
Given the current political situation in Myanmar, implementation of this judgment will likely require the cooperation of actors beyond Myanmar’s central government, including the Arakan Army, a nonstate armed group that now controls much of Rakhine State and has also been inflicting abuse on the Rohingyas. Myanmar remains legally responsible for carrying out the restitution ordered by the court and for upholding its obligations under the Genocide Convention, which include preventing and punishing genocide. The court found that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide by civilians acting alongside its security forces, so that duty reaches beyond the state’s own agents. An assurance of safe return from Naypyidaw means little to families going back to townships the Arakan Army controls.
Bangladesh, where more than one million Rohingya refugees now live, seems to have already considered its next diplomatic moves. On November 8, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam talked about engaging with both the Myanmar authorities and the Arakan Army. She raised concerns regarding the wide-ranging opposition in Myanmar to the return of the Rohingyas. This suggests that the Arakan Army’s capture of most of Rakhine from the military, on its own, will not clear the path for the refugees’ return. While the ICJ judgment bolsters the case for a durable return, Dhaka’s negotiations with various actors in Myanmar should continue.
India, too, has interests in Myanmar, in part because of its connectivity ambitions. The port in Sittwe and the Kaladan corridor are part of its Act East strategy to connect the landlocked northeastern states to the Bay of Bengal region. Local businesses are already dealing directly with the Arakan Army, which now holds the territory across the border. On October 31, a Times of India report mentioned a trade agreement between the Siaha district unit of the Mizoram Commercial Vehicles Association and the Arakan Army’s political wing. Indian engagement with Myanmar has been under consideration for a while. As a former Indian ambassador to Myanmar put it last year, “The Chinese openly have relations with all sides; can India afford not to have the same?” Therefore, New Delhi’s reaction to the ICJ judgment appears restrained. While it acknowledged the verdict and supported a sustainable return, it did not use the word genocide.
Citizenship disputes also shape India’s bilateral relations with Bangladesh. After the National Register of Citizens (NRC) exercise left out 1.9 million people from a citizenship registry, the United Nations Refugee Agency warned in September 2019 about the risk of indefinite statelessness. At the time, rights groups warned that it could set off a crisis like the one the Rohingya faced in Myanmar in 2017. The broader geopolitical concern for the region is much about how states distinguish their own citizens from populations they regard as foreign, particularly those communities that are deemed to share ethnic, linguistic, or religious characteristics across the border. Bangladesh has a direct stake in the consequences of this kind of citizenship framing by its two neighbors.
For their part, Chinese policymakers are focused on different kinds of issues when it comes to Myanmar. As Crisis Group has noted, Beijing has long cultivated ties with numerous groups in the country, including the Arakan Army. Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative and Kyaukphyu goals mean that China has an interest in securing a negotiation between armed actors and the Myanmar authorities. Not surprisingly, while Beijing responded to the ICJ judgment with concern regarding judicial overreach, it offered continued support for dialogue. That keeps China positioned as an intermediary without committing it to enforcement, though Beijing is hardly neutral. Crisis Group notes that it threw the military regime a lifeline in 2024. Bangladesh’s challenge is to obtain Chinese backing for repatriation without Beijing treating the Rohingya’s return as something to settle only after its commercial projects are secure.
The role of the United States reflects another set of tensions. While Washington recognized the Myanmar military’s atrocities as genocide in 2022, its current diplomatic priorities appear to have shifted. As Reuters reported earlier this month, a State Department strategy seeks a ceasefire offering a pathway to peace by 2030, through forums on fiscal federalism and territorial demarcation that it links to access to Myanmar’s rare earths. Washington’s reaction to the ICJ verdict laid out concerns for abuses, and at the same time it noted its concern about “politicization” of the court. The question remains as to whether Washington will prioritize citizenship of the Rohingyas or make it a lower priority compared to its commercial opportunities.
Bangladesh has proposed the UN General Assembly as a platform for mobilizing support and building a coalition to press Myanmar and the Arakan Army to carry out the court’s restitution measures, not least since the country now holds the rotating General Assembly presidency. Along its border with Rakhine state, Bangladesh can expand trade as an incentive for further cooperation. Such tools create openings for negotiations. It is crucial that Rohingya representatives and youth participate in such dialogues when it comes to securing full citizenship rights and future repatriations, with the backing of the international community.
Next, the court ruled that Myanmar must report within two years regarding measures it has adopted to provide restitution and, if applicable, compensation. But there is a risk in moving too fast. Negotiations that result in a hurried repatriation that leaves the Rohingya vulnerable could lead to instability, forced exodus, and ultimately additional atrocities. While the ICJ judgment provides Bangladesh and its partners a diplomatic opportunity, international partners must press for a secure Rohingya citizenship status in Myanmar before embarking on future steps.

title: China’s Cargo Drones Keep Getting Bigger With New W8000
zh_title: 新型 W8000 助力中国货运无人机不断发展壮大
summary: 中国部署越来越大的无人货运飞机的野心正在不断增强，白鲸航空推出了 W8000 货运无人机，据报道，这款货运无人机设计可承载 8 吨（略低于 18,000 磅）。该飞机代表了该公司自主货运航空计划的重大扩展，恰逢其较小的 W5000 已开始飞行测试。参观者在珠海 W8000 前合影。来自中国互联网 W5000（左）停在珠海的 W8000 旁边。来自中国互联网 W8000先于中国国际航空展亮相珠海
content:
中国部署越来越大的无人货运飞机的野心正在不断增强，白鲸航空推出了 W8000 货运无人机，据报道，这款货运无人机设计可承载 8 吨（略低于 18,000 磅）。该飞机代表了该公司自主货运航空计划的重大扩展，恰逢其较小的 W5000 已开始飞行测试。参观者在珠海 W8000 前合影。来自中国互联网 W5000（左）停在珠海的 W8000 旁边。来自中国互联网 W8000 在中国国际航空航天博览会（俗称中国航展）之前亮相珠海。在 12 月 7 日该活动开幕之前，我们已经抢先了解了一个平台，该平台旨在将无人货运能力提升到目前仅限于传统载人运输机的水平。据报道，其有效载荷为 8 吨，远高于 W5000，后者的设计载荷可达 5 吨（11,000 磅）。与 W5000 一样，W8000 可以通过后坡道装卸。 W8000 尾部的翻盖式门和后装载坡道。然而目前，双涡轮螺旋桨飞机 W8000 仍然是一个开发概念。其有效载荷数字只是设计目标，其航程、最大起飞重量和操作要求等细节仍不清楚。
为了进行比较，八吨的有效载荷将使 W8000 与 DHC-5 Buffalo 双引擎涡轮螺旋桨短距起降运输机处于同一类别。无论如何，此次亮相凸显了白鲸航空开发一系列大型无人驾驶货运飞机的雄心，目标是区域货运、偏远地区物流和潜在的军事运输任务，在这些任务中，自主飞机可以比传统货运业务提供优势。珠海W8000的后视图。来自中国互联网 双涡轮螺旋桨飞机 W8000 动力装置所使用的发动机尚未确定。通过中国互联网 更大的无人运输 W8000 的有效负载能力将使其能够运输大型设备、托盘货物、工业用品和其他大件货物。在商业环境中，大型自主货运飞机在公路或铁路基础设施有限或传统航空运输过于昂贵而无法频繁运营的航线上特别有用。尽管消除了机上机组人员，但飞机仍然需要维护人员、地勤人员、货物装载基础设施和支持性运营网络。最终，该飞机也可能被批准在受控空域内运行，取代载人支线货运业务，但这种用例在未来仍有一段路要走。不可避免的是，该飞机的发展也表明了大型货运无人机的潜在军事意义。
珠海的 W5000 和 W8000。来自中国互联网 W8000 可以为中国人民解放军 (PLA) 提供大量额外的空运选择，以保障在偏远、孤立或基础设施匮乏的地点作战的部队。这在印度-太平洋地区尤其重要，中国不断扩大的军事设施和岛屿前哨网络已经对频繁的补给飞行产生了需求。例如，在南中国海，大型货运无人机可以将设备、医疗用品、备件和其他必需品运输到远程设施，而无需载人运输

【原文 English Original】
China’s ambitions to field increasingly large, uncrewed cargo aircraft are growing, with Air White Whale unveiling its W8000, a cargo UAV reportedly designed to carry up to eight metric tons — a little less than 18,000 pounds. The aircraft represents a significant expansion of the company’s plans for autonomous freight aviation, coming just as its smaller W5000 has begun flight testing. Visitors pose in front of the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet The W5000 (left) parked next to the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet The W8000 appeared in Zhuhai, ahead of the China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, commonly known as Airshow China . Before that event opens its doors on December 7, we have gotten an early look at a platform intended to push uncrewed cargo capacity into a class now limited to conventional, crewed transport aircraft. Its reported eight-ton payload would put it substantially above the W5000, which is designed to carry up to five metric tons (11,000 pounds). Like the W5000, the W8000 can be loaded and unloaded via a rear ramp. Clamshell doors and rear loading ramp in the tail of the W8000. via Chinese internet For now, however, the twin-turboprop W8000 remains a developmental concept. Its payload figure is a design target, and details about its range, maximum takeoff weight, and operational requirements are still unclear. For purposes of comparison, an eight-metric-ton payload would put the W8000 in much the same category as the DHC-5 Buffalo twin-engine turboprop STOL transport. Regardless, the unveiling highlights Air White Whale’s ambitions to develop a family of large uncrewed cargo aircraft, targeting regional freight, remote-area logistics, and potentially military transportation missions where autonomous aircraft could offer advantages over conventional cargo operations. Rear view of the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet The engines used in the powerplant for the twin-turboprop W8000 are yet to be identified. via Chinese internet An Even Bigger Uncrewed Transport The W8000’s payload capacity would allow it to transport large equipment, palletized freight, industrial supplies, and other bulky cargo. In a commercial context, large autonomous cargo aircraft could be particularly useful on routes where road or rail infrastructure is limited, or where conventional air transport is too expensive to operate frequently. Although eliminating onboard flight crews, the aircraft would still require maintenance personnel, ground handling, cargo-loading infrastructure, and a supporting operational network. Ultimately, the aircraft could also be cleared to operate inside controlled airspace, displacing crewed feeder cargo operations, but that use case is still some way off in the future. Inevitably, the aircraft’s development also points toward the potential military relevance of large cargo UAVs. The W5000 and W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet The W8000 could offer the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) a substantial additional airlift option for sustaining forces operating from remote, isolated, or infrastructure-poor locations. This is particularly relevant in the Indo-Pacific, where China’s expanding network of military facilities and island outposts is already creating demand for frequent resupply flights. In the South China Sea, for example, large cargo UAVs could potentially transport equipment, medical supplies, spare parts, and other necessities to remote installations without requiring a crewed transport aircraft for every mission. They could also support operations in western China , including remote and high-altitude regions where road infrastructure is limited and conventional air transport can face additional challenges. There are also potential applications in a conflict, where conventional logistics infrastructure could be damaged or otherwise unavailable. Uncrewed transports would remove the risk to aircrews during routine resupply missions through contested airspace, although the aircraft themselves would remain vulnerable. They would also remove the need for combat search and rescue (CSAR) capabilities, which might be impossible to provide in at least some scenarios. Their usefulness would also depend, at least in some cases, on reliable communications, autonomous navigation, and the ability to operate without continuous access to satellite navigation. Profile view of the W8000 at Zhuhai. via Chinese internet W5000 Has Already Begun Flight Testing The W8000’s unveiling comes as Air White Whale’s smaller W5000 has reached a significant development milestone, completing its maiden flight on November 14. The five-ton cargo UAV reportedly conducted a roughly 30-minute test flight after taking off within approximately 600 meters (1,969 feet). During the flight, it reportedly conducted maneuvers and tested autonomous flight functions, datalink communications, propulsion, and flight-control systems before landing. China’s W5000 large cargo UAV has completed its maiden flight in the Ordos region of Inner Mongolia on 14 November. The aircraft reportedly took off after a 600 m (1,969 ft) ground run, climbed to 2,000 m (6,562 ft) and completed a 30-minute test flight. The trial included… pic.twitter.com/NNLqPKbLLZ — Drone Wars (@Drone_Wars_) November 14, 2026 The W5000 is designed to carry up to five metric tons of cargo, with a reported maximum range of 2,600 kilometers (1,616 miles), maximum takeoff weight of 10.8 tons (21,600 pounds), and cargo compartment volume exceeding 65 cubic meters (2,295 cubic feet). The aircraft is powered by twin turboprop engines. Chinese sources claim that Air White Whale has received 835 orders or prospective commitments from domestic logistics companies for the W5000, although the nature of those commitments and how many represent firm purchase contracts remain unclear. Commercial operations are currently planned to begin by the end of 2027, subject to further testing and certification. The W5000’s flight provides an indication of the company’s progress toward developing large uncrewed cargo aircraft, but the W8000 is a considerably more ambitious undertaking. Several other companies are also pursuing increasingly ambitious uncrewed transport aircraft. These include Tengden’s four-engine TB-001D Scorpion D , which first flew in October 2022 and is designed to carry up to 1.5 metric tons (3,307 pounds) of cargo, as well as the Star UAV System-developed AT200, another 1.5-ton-class cargo drone. The TB0D Scorpion D built by China’s Tengden Technology company completed its maiden flight in Sichuan on October 25, 2022. Twitter video screenshot Other designs include the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China’s HH-100 , with a reported payload capacity of around 700 kilograms (1,543 pounds), and the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation’s CH-YH1000 , designed to carry approximately one metric ton (2,205 pounds). While these aircraft vary considerably in size, configuration, and intended missions, their development highlights China’s broader push to establish uncrewed cargo aviation as a viable logistics capability. A demonstrator of China’s HH-100 commercial cargo drone. Photo by Yue Shuhua/VCG via Getty Images VCG Outside of China, there is some other notable activity in this sector. The United States is also pursuing large uncrewed cargo aircraft for military logistics. As we reported , Textron Aviation and autonomy specialist Merlin recently unveiled the Cessna SkyCourier UX, a concept based on the twin-engine Cessna 408 SkyCourier. The proposed aircraft would use Merlin’s autonomous flight system and could carry approximately 6,000 pounds of cargo. Its designers are exploring a cockpit-less configuration with a hydraulically opening nose section for direct cargo loading, as well as kneeling landing gear and integrated loading systems to simplify operations at austere locations. With a reported range of around 900 nautical miles, the SkyCourier UX is intended to support distributed military forces, including across the Pacific, where it could move supplies between larger logistics hubs and smaller, remote operating locations. The U.S. Air Force has also experimented with autonomous Cessna Caravan aircraft through Joby Aviation and its former Xwing autonomy team, including logistics demonstrations across the Pacific. Better known for land vehicles, Oshkosh Defense also recently announced a partnership with Silicon Valley startup Grid Aero, with the aim of building large military cargo drones. These would draw upon Grid Aero’s experience developing the Lifter family, an autonomous aircraft series with modular payload capacity that the company describes as a “pickup truck of the skies.” The Lifter is planned to carry somewhere between 1,000 and 8,000 pounds over a distance of approximately 1,500 miles.  The Grid Aero Lifter. Oshkosh/Grid Aero While the United States is moving slower than China in this space, there is arguably an even stronger operational case for such capabilities in the U.S. military, given the expeditionary nature of a potential conflict across the vast distances of the Indo-Pacific . Sustaining forces spread across widely separated islands, remote airfields, and austere forward operating locations would place enormous demands on conventional airlift and sealift networks. China Targets A New Class Of Cargo Aviation Overall, the development of the W5000 and W8000 highlights China’s growing interest in cargo UAVs capable of moving freight measured in metric tons rather than kilograms. While smaller delivery drones are increasingly being explored for last-mile transportation, aircraft such as the W8000 are aimed at moving substantial loads between logistics hubs without requiring an onboard crew. If the W8000 progresses, it could eventually offer a heavier transport option alongside the W5000, allowing Air White Whale to target different cargo requirements and routes. The W5000 and W8000 at Zhuhai ahead of Airshow China. via Chinese internet For now, the W8000 points to where Air White Whale wants to take its cargo UAV program. The W5000’s flight-test program will be an important step in establishing whether the company can turn its designs into operational aircraft and start to offer a new class of uncrewed airlift.
